'Two offers,' Deepak said, dropping onto Vaibhav's bed. 'Startup A: sixty hours a week, unpaid, and they said "we'll see about a job later". Startup B: thirty hours, a small stipend, and a mentor.'

'Sixty? But A is the big name.'

'Last month I wrote three words on my wall. Honesty. Learning. Family time.' Deepak pointed at the paper. 'So I'm asking each offer the same three questions.'

'And?'

'A: their ad says flexible hours and it isn't, so honesty, no. Learning, maybe, but nobody would teach me. Family time, zero. Sunday lunch is gone.'

'And B?'

'B fits all three.'

'So you'll say no to A?'

'Already typed the email.'

qa.q: Which three values did Deepak write on the wall?
qa.a: Deepak wrote honesty, learning and family time.

qa.q: How does Deepak feel about turning down Startup A?
qa.a: Deepak feels settled and sure, since the email was already typed.

qa.q: What could Deepak do if Startup B also starts asking for more hours?
qa.a: Deepak could ask the same three questions again and talk to the mentor about limits before agreeing.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see Deepak's approach?
qa.a: Vaibhav may find it surprising since A is the big name, but may respect that Deepak used clear reasons.

grounding: Shows a student testing internship offers against a short list of values and refusing the one that would erode them.

passage: I'm Pranav, and the summer of my third year I had two internship offers. One was at a big-name media house. The other was at a small community radio station. Before I replied, my friend Jaya made me do something odd: write three things I actually care about. I wrote: honesty, learning, family time. Then I checked each offer against them. The media house wanted me in from nine to nine, six days, with no stipend, and the senior said, "Everyone here stays late, it's how you prove yourself." That would eat family time completely, and I'd be too tired to learn much. The radio station was shorter hours, and they promised I'd actually edit shows. I emailed the media house a polite no. My mother couldn't believe I'd turned down the famous one.

qa.q: What hours did the media house want Pranav to work?
qa.a: From nine to nine, six days, with no stipend.

qa.q: How do you think Pranav felt emailing the polite no?
qa.a: Pranav probably felt nervous about turning down a famous name, but also clear and relieved because the choice matched the values on the list.

qa.q: What else could Pranav check before accepting the radio station offer?
qa.a: Talk to a past intern there about whether they really got to edit shows, so learning is tested, not just promised.

qa.q: How might Pranav's mother see the decision?
qa.a: She is surprised and maybe worried that the famous name was turned down, though she might come round once she hears the reasons.

grounding: A student writes down honesty, learning and family time and rejects an internship with long unpaid hours that would erode them.

Placement cell counsellor's note, Tuesday

Aadhya came in today with two internship offers and a sheet of paper. At the top she had written three words: honesty, learning, family time. She had drawn a column for each offer and ticked or crossed each value. One firm offered a big name but no stipend and expected interns till eleven at night; a senior had also told her to "round up" survey numbers for a client. She crossed out honesty and family time for that one. The other, a smaller research lab with fair hours, had ticks for all three. Her classmate Madhav had taken the first firm last year and warned her about it. I asked her to confirm the lab's hours in writing. She will reply to both firms by Friday.

qa.q: What three words did Aadhya write at the top of her sheet?
What might Aadhya have felt when a senior told her to 'round up' survey numbers?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable and uneasy, since it clashed with honesty, one of her three values.

qa.q: What could Aadhya do if the lab's written hours turn out longer than promised?
qa.a: She could ask the lab to explain before accepting, and weigh it against her list again rather than deciding on impulse.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel seeing Aadhya use his warning?
qa.a: Madhav would probably feel glad his bad experience helped someone else avoid it.

grounding: A student checks internship offers against her values and rejects one with long unpaid hours that would erode them.
